cv.alt: Tolgee supplying content to a Next.js page, which also renders a PDF built by Chromium, and publishes contact messages to Kafka for the shared notifications service to deliver.
cv.caption: The same content renders twice: an editorial page for a person, and a single-column document for a parser. Building the PDF at compile time is what keeps its text real rather than a picture of text.

designSystem.alt: The design system in three layers — tokens, then components that reference only tokens, then per-product themes — vendored as a copy into each consumer.
designSystem.caption: Themes override colour and nothing else. Shape, type scale and spacing stay on shared tokens, so a full reskin touches no component file.

gpool.alt: The gpool request path: a Next.js front end calling a NestJS API backed by Postgres, with the API publishing email intent to Kafka for the shared notifications service to deliver.
gpool.caption: The API publishes an email intent and moves on. Delivery, idempotency and dead-lettering belong to a service that already does them, so joining a pool never waits on an SMTP call.

kini.alt: kini, and the practices extracted from it — the translation workflow, release automation and compose layout — carried into the repositories that followed.
kini.caption: Kept as its own repository rather than folded into gpool, so the rewrite could change its mind about the architecture without rewriting history.

notifications.alt: A delivery pipeline reading a versioned topic through a consumer, idempotency claims and locale-resolved templates to a sent email, with malformed payloads branching off to a dead-letter record.
notifications.caption: Invalid payloads fail as non-retryable and land in a durable record. Retrying a malformed message forever is a worse outcome than losing it loudly.

platformOps.alt: The products attached to one shared Docker network, which fronts three families of service: secrets and translations, events, and observability.
platformOps.caption: Seven of the eleven services are observability. That ratio is deliberate: the expensive part of running several small services is not running them, it is being able to see them.

sity.alt: A road plan feeding a network builder that produces both the directed lane graph and the drawn scene, with the verification reading the graph back through the page.
sity.caption: Roads are drawn from the graph rather than the graph fitted to the drawing, so a vehicle on lane data is on the asphalt.

tradingBot.caption: Backtesting and live execution consume the same strategy crate, so a result that cannot be reproduced offline is a bug rather than a mystery.

cv.approach: One source of content, rendered twice. The page is an editorial layout with a case study behind each project; the same data renders a separate single-column document that headless Chromium turns into a PDF during the build, so the parsed version keeps real selectable text rather than a picture of it.
decisions: The PDF is generated at build time rather than in the browser. Client-side html-to-PDF libraries rasterise the page, destroying the selectable text the entire ATS layout exists to produce.

Nothing it publishes carries a way to reach a person directly. The contact form reaches the same inbox through a secret held in OpenBao, so no address appears in the page, the PDF or the structured data.
The contact endpoint sends RFC 9457 problem details like the four APIs, so one error shape covers the whole estate rather than four.

pieces.text: Every word lives in Tolgee under a cv.* namespace — the case studies, the section names and the PDF headings included. What stays in code is only what reads identically in every language: ids, ordering and technology names.
pieces.title: Content

pieces.text: Next.js in standalone output, with the locale resolved on the server from a cookie, then Accept-Language, then the default, so the tab title and the search snippet follow the selected language rather than lagging a request behind it.
pieces.title: The page

pieces.text: A separate print document built for extraction — one column, conventional headings, no icons, contact details in plain text — rendered by Chromium during the Docker build, which fails if the file cannot be produced.
pieces.title: The PDF

automation: Dependabot opens grouped pull requests once a week and waits seven days before proposing a newly published version. A compromised release is usually caught and yanked within days, and nothing here is urgent enough to be worth installing first.

Auto-merge is enabled on every non-draft pull request the moment it opens, which leaves branch protection as the only thing holding it: green checks merge, red ones sit. Dependabot majors are the one exclusion, because a major is a change to read rather than a number to bump.
CodeQL, dependency review and Semgrep run on every pull request, and the SBOM is kept as an artefact of each one rather than only of a release.
The PDF is rendered by headless Chromium inside the Docker build, which fails if the file cannot be produced. A deploy cannot ship a page and a stale PDF that disagree with each other.

The deploy bundle is the repository at the released commit, so the host runs the deploy script belonging to the release it is deploying. Rolling back to an older tag restores that release's deploy logic with it, rather than running today's script against last month's compose file.

Local development has two modes over one set of containers. `local:up` runs the production image, so what is being checked is what ships; `local:dev` builds a dev stage instead and runs `next dev` under `docker compose watch`, which copies changed files into the running container rather than rebuilding it. The rebuild it skips includes the Chromium PDF render, the slowest step in the image.

stages.text: Husky runs gitleaks over the staged diff, then lint, typecheck, the unit suite and build, so a workspace that does not compile or pass its tests never becomes a branch. commitlint holds the message to Conventional Commits — release-please reads those later to decide the version — and a pre-push hook refuses to push to main at all.
stages.title: Before the commit

stages.text: Six jobs in parallel: quality (format, lint, typecheck, unit tests and build), a full-repository secret scan, a Docker smoke that boots the production image and probes it, Playwright asserting WCAG 2.1 AA and Core Web Vitals budgets in a real browser, licences with a production-only audit alongside an SBOM and Trivy, and Semgrep. A run superseded by a newer commit is cancelled rather than left holding a runner.
stages.title: The pull request

stages.text: release-please keeps a release pull request open against main, deriving the next version and the changelog from the conventional commits since the last tag. Merging it tags and publishes the release, so cutting one is a merge rather than a command somebody runs on a laptop.
stages.title: The release

stages.text: A published release builds the image, pushes it to ECR and has cosign sign it keylessly by digest with SLSA provenance attached — by digest, because a tag can be repointed after signing. The compose bundle goes to S3 and SSM runs the deploy script on the EC2 host, so no runner ever holds an SSH key.
stages.title: The deploy

cv.problem: A CV is read by two audiences that want opposite things. A person wants something worth looking at; an applicant tracking system wants one column of plain text under conventional headings. Serving either one well usually breaks the other.
cv.tagline: This site: a CV that renders itself twice, once for a person and once for a parser.

design-system.approach: Components are plain React styled only through CSS custom properties, with no Tailwind, no CSS-in-JS and no build step. Any of the three can import them as-is, and each supplies its own theme file rather than editing component source.
decisions: Themes override colour only. Shape, type scale and spacing stay on shared base tokens, so every product renders identical geometry and differs solely in paint.
Vendored into each consumer rather than published as a package: the products are private and a copy keeps the dependency graph flat.

pieces.text: Colour, typography, spacing, radius, shadow and motion as oklch-based custom properties, with one neutral default theme.
pieces.title: Tokens

pieces.text: Primitives grouped by concern — core, forms, feedback, data-display, navigation, overlay, icons — each referencing tokens only, never a literal colour.
pieces.title: Components

pieces.text: One file per product overriding colour tokens. A full reskin touches zero component files.
pieces.title: Themes

automation: The manifest is generated, and CI fails when the committed one differs from a fresh run. A hand-edited manifest is how a component quietly disappears from the list every consumer reads.

Every component in the manifest is mounted and run through axe in the test run, and the specimen pages are checked in a real browser, so a component that no longer renders — or a token pairing that fails contrast — fails here rather than in whichever product upgrades first.
Dependabot on npm and the Actions; the components themselves have no runtime dependencies to update.
A secret scan and Semgrep on every pull request, the same two gates as everywhere else — a repository with no build is not a repository with no risk.

stages.text: No build, no bundle and nothing for a consumer to install — this is components, tokens and guidelines that other repositories vendor. So CI checks the things that can actually go wrong: a leaked secret, a manifest that no longer matches what is on disk, and a component or a token pairing that fails accessibility. The manifest has to be regenerated rather than hand-edited, every component listed in it is mounted and run through axe, the JSON files are parsed, and Playwright opens every specimen page in Chromium to check WCAG A and AA — colour contrast included, which only exists where layout and paint do.
stages.title: The pull request

stages.text: release-please cuts a version from the conventional commits. That tag is the entire distribution: products depend on the repository at a pinned tag, so there is no registry publish to fail and no unpublished version to chase.
stages.title: The release

stages.text: A design system release deploys nothing by itself. Each product picks it up when its own Dependabot bumps the pinned tag, and it then ships through that product's pipeline — which is why a component change reaches each product on that product's schedule rather than all at once.
stages.title: The upgrade

design-system.problem: Three products had drifted into three styling technologies — plain CSS classes, Tailwind utilities and CVA variants — and no shared visual language. Picking one framework would have meant rewriting two applications.
design-system.tagline: A technology-agnostic token and component library three products share without agreeing on a CSS framework.

gpool.approach: One monorepo with a NestJS API and a Next.js web app, both joining a shared platform rather than owning their own infrastructure. Secrets, translations, the event broker and observability all come from platform-ops; gpool ships only the two containers that are actually its own.
decisions: Secrets are fetched at boot by a wrapper process, never baked into an image or committed to an env file, so a leaked app token exposes one kv path rather than the whole store.
Email is an event, not a call. The API publishes to a topic and a shared service owns delivery, idempotency and dead-lettering.
CI regenerates the web API contract from the running API and fails on drift, so client and server cannot disagree silently.

Errors are RFC 9457 problem details with a translatable code, and every route declares its status code — which is how it came out that Nest was answering 201 to POSTs the generated client documented as 200.

pieces.text: NestJS monolith covering auth, pools and RUM. It owns the Google OAuth exchange and issues the session itself, so the client secret lives in one service rather than two. Runs database migrations on startup, exposes an OpenAPI spec, and publishes email intent as Kafka events rather than sending mail itself.
pieces.title: API

pieces.text: Next.js App Router in standalone output, talking to the API directly with a session cookie rather than proxying every call to sign its own headers. Translations are pulled from Tolgee at boot; the container starts under a wrapper that fetches its secrets from OpenBao and refuses to boot without the keys it declares.
pieces.title: Web

pieces.text: Images build to ECR on release, a bundle lands in S3, and SSM drives a compose deploy on the shared EC2 host. CI gates on lint, typecheck, coverage, a compose integration smoke, gitleaks, SBOM and a Trivy scan.
pieces.title: Delivery

automation: Translations promote themselves. A push to main touching the message files, the Tolgee config or the production env promotes the copy to the production Tolgee project, so wording ships without a release.
Dependabot watches four ecosystems — npm, both Dockerfiles and the Actions themselves — grouped weekly, with patch and minor merging on green and majors left for a person.
The public endpoints are probed every five minutes from outside the estate by platform-ops, which opens an issue when one stops answering.
CodeQL, dependency review and Semgrep on every pull request; Trivy and the SBOM again at deploy, against the image that is actually shipping rather than the one CI happened to build.

Local development has two modes over one set of containers. `local:up` runs the production images; `local:dev` builds a dev stage of each and runs `nest start --watch` and `next dev` under `docker compose watch`, so an edit reaches the running container as a file sync instead of an image rebuild. Dependency manifests still trigger a rebuild, because a lockfile change cannot be copied in.

stages.text: The same three hooks every repository here carries: gitleaks over the staged diff followed by lint, typecheck, build and both unit suites; commitlint on the message; and a pre-push hook that refuses main. CI sets HUSKY=0 so the hooks never run a second time on a runner that is already running them as jobs.
stages.title: Before the commit

stages.text: Five jobs: quality — compose manifests rendered, lint, typecheck, build, API unit tests with coverage uploaded and the web suite — a secret scan, an integration smoke that stands the whole stack up under Compose and then opens a real browser on it — the sign-in page rendered, axe against WCAG A and AA, Core Web Vitals budgets — before a k6 load smoke, security and supply chain, and Semgrep.
stages.title: The pull request

stages.text: release-please derives the version and the changelog from the conventional commits on main, and publishes the tag when its pull request is merged.
stages.title: The release

stages.text: Both images are built, Trivy-scanned before they leave the runner, then signed with cosign and given SLSA provenance and an SBOM attestation, all bound to the digest. S3 carries the bundle, SSM applies it on the host, and a post-deploy smoke hits the public health endpoint — the only check that can fail after production has already changed.
stages.title: The deploy

gpool.problem: A prediction pool needs more than a spreadsheet: authentication, scoring that settles on a schedule, notifications, and a record of why anyone holds the points they do. Every one of those is a service, and standing them up per project does not scale.
gpool.tagline: A real-time football pool platform: private pools, live scoring, and an auditable trail of every point.

kini.approach: A NestJS API and Next.js client in one monorepo, with monitoring wired in locally. Much of what it worked out — the compose layout, the Tolgee translation flow, the release and deploy workflows — became the template the later projects started from.
decisions: Kept as its own repository rather than folded into gpool, so the rewrite could change its mind about the architecture without rewriting history.

Errors are RFC 9457 problem details with a translatable code, and resources are plural and nested: a match now lives under the pool that owns it, and the pool in the path is checked rather than decorative.

pieces.text: NestJS backend and Next.js client, sharing a compose stack and a single set of CI workflows.
pieces.title: API and web

pieces.text: The translation workflow, the commit and release automation, and the local-first compose layout were all extracted and reused rather than rebuilt.
pieces.title: What carried forward

automation: A proof of concept runs the same pipeline as production. The point of owning the template is that a new idea starts with signed images, a smoke test and a changelog rather than earning them later, when retrofitting is exactly what nobody has time for.
Dependabot across npm, both Dockerfiles and the Actions, grouped weekly, with patch and minor merging on green.
CodeQL, dependency review and Semgrep on every pull request.

Local development has two modes over one set of containers. `local:up` runs the production images; `local:dev` builds a dev stage of each and runs `nest start --watch` and `next dev` under `docker compose watch`, so an edit reaches the running container as a file sync instead of an image rebuild. Dependency manifests still trigger a rebuild, because a lockfile change cannot be copied in.

stages.text: gitleaks over the staged diff, then lint, typecheck and build; commitlint on the message; and a pre-push hook that refuses main.

stages.text: Quality, a secret scan, an integration smoke that stands the API, the web app and Postgres up under Compose from the production images and then drives the web in a real browser — the sign-in card rendered, axe against WCAG A and AA, Core Web Vitals budgets — security and supply chain, and Semgrep.

stages.text: API and web images built and pushed, signed with cosign by digest with SLSA provenance attached, bundled to S3, applied on the host through SSM, then smoke-tested against the public health endpoint.

kini.problem: The original attempt at a pool platform: teams, invitations, and scoring, built before there was any shared infrastructure to lean on.
kini.tagline: The first football pool platform, and the one that taught me what gpool needed to be.

notifications.approach: One consumer owns delivery for all of them. Producers publish an intent event and stop caring; the service validates the contract, renders a localised template, sends it, and keeps a durable record of every attempt.
decisions: Invalid payloads fail as non-retryable and go to a durable dead-letter record, because retrying a malformed message forever is a worse outcome than losing it loudly.
A versioned topic name, so a contract change is a new topic rather than a silent break for every producer.
Errors are RFC 9457 problem details like every other service, even though this one serves nothing but health and metrics — the 404s and 500s it does emit are the ones nobody writes a client for.

pieces.text: Reads a versioned topic under a stable consumer group and validates every event against an explicit contract, rejecting malformed payloads as non-retryable rather than looping on them.
pieces.title: Consumer

pieces.text: Atomic idempotency claims stop duplicate sends, and processing leases let a crashed worker’s in-flight messages be picked up rather than stranded.
pieces.title: Delivery

pieces.text: Handlebars templates keyed by source application and template id, resolved per locale, with data escaped on render so sender-controlled content cannot inject markup.
pieces.title: Templates

automation: Compose manifests are rendered in CI, so a file that no longer parses fails on the pull request rather than on the host, halfway through a deploy.
The integration job dumps the container logs when it fails. A red run without them only tells you to reproduce it locally, which is the slowest possible way to learn what the broker did.
Dependabot on npm, the Dockerfile and the Actions, weekly and grouped; patch and minor merge on green.
CodeQL, dependency review and Semgrep on every pull request.

Local development has two modes over one container. `local:up` runs the production image; `local:dev` builds a dev stage and runs `nest start --watch` under `docker compose watch`, so an edit to the worker reaches it as a file sync instead of an image rebuild. Dependency manifests still trigger a rebuild, because a lockfile change cannot be copied in.

stages.text: gitleaks over the staged diff, then lint, typecheck and build; commitlint on the message; and a pre-push hook that refuses main.
stages.title: Before the commit

stages.text: Six jobs, one of which is the one that matters: the service runs against a real Kafka, a real PostgreSQL and an SMTP sink. Idempotency and dead-lettering are claims about what a broker does under redelivery, and a mocked broker will agree with whatever the code already believes.
stages.title: The pull request

stages.text: release-please, with the version mirrored into the API package and its lockfile entry so the artefact and the tag cannot drift apart.
stages.title: The release

stages.text: The API image is built and pushed, signed with cosign by digest with SLSA provenance attached, bundled to S3 and applied on the host through SSM.
stages.title: The deploy

notifications.problem: Every product eventually needs to send mail, and every product that does it inline reinvents retries, deduplication and the question of what happened to a message that never arrived.
notifications.tagline: A Kafka-backed email service the other products delegate delivery to, with idempotency and crash recovery built in.

platform-ops.approach: One ops stack, one external Docker network, and a rule that applications own only their own containers. An app declares which secret path it reads and which topics it uses; everything underneath is shared and versioned in one place.
decisions: Per-application OpenBao policies scoped to exactly one kv path, so an app token is useless against any other app.
The same compose manifests describe local and production, so a local reproduction is a real reproduction.

The whole estate runs on one host by design, which leaves cost a single lever: stop it. A scheduled window and a manual switch turn production off for the hours nobody uses it, and everything comes back on its own from the disk.

One HTTP contract for five services: RFC 9457 problem details carrying a translatable code, plural nested resources, explicit status codes per verb, and a URL version only where a separately deployed service is the caller.

pieces.text: One external Docker network, platform_ops_shared. An application joins it, resolves every shared service by container alias, and needs to know nothing else about the topology. There is no service mesh and no discovery layer — joining the network is the whole contract, which is why every repository creates it before anything else starts.
pieces.title: The integration seam

pieces.text: OpenBao holds every application secret behind a policy scoped to exactly one kv path, and a boot wrapper fetches them and refuses to start a container missing a key it declared. It unseals itself from a KMS key nothing else on the host can reach, so a reboot no longer leaves production without secrets. Tolgee holds the copy, which applications pull as a snapshot at build time and merge live at request time. Unleash holds the switches behind its own domain on the shared ingress, reached by applications over the internal network: an application declares which flags it has and what they default to, and the server supplies values, so losing it degrades to those defaults rather than to an outage.
pieces.title: Secrets, translations and flags

pieces.text: Redpanda speaks the Kafka API without a JVM or ZooKeeper, carrying versioned topics such as notification.email.requested.v1 — how an application hands off an email instead of sending one itself. A console for browsing topics, consumer groups and messages runs locally only; production has no reason to expose it.
pieces.title: Events

pieces.text: Traces are pushed by the application to an OTel collector and stored in Jaeger. Metrics are scraped the other way round — Prometheus reaches into each application on a schedule, and routes whatever fires to Alertmanager. Logs need no participation at all: Alloy tails them off the host into Loki, so applications only ever write to stdout. Grafana reads the last two and is the one place anyone actually looks. Every alert carries the environment that raised it, so production is never mistaken for a laptop.
pieces.title: Three signals, three paths

pieces.text: Commit hooks that scan for secrets, parse every workflow, render every compose file and check Terraform formatting before anything reaches CI.
pieces.title: Guardrails

automation: An uptime probe runs every five minutes on GitHub's infrastructure and checks the public health endpoints from outside. Prometheus runs on the same host as the things it watches, so it cannot report its own death — and the silence looks exactly like everything being fine.
The probe opens a GitHub issue rather than sending mail. An issue deduplicates, carries a state, and does not depend on the SMTP relay, which is itself one of the things that could be broken.
Scheduled runs are best effort by design: GitHub delays them under load and skips them outright on a busy account, so this is roughly every five minutes and never a heartbeat.
Dependabot on npm and the Actions, weekly and grouped, with patch and minor merging on green.

A Power workflow stops and starts the single production host on demand, and two EventBridge Scheduler rules do the same on a fixed daily window. Off means a stopped machine, not a torn-down one: every database, the secret store and the certificates stay on its volume, and the uptime probe reads the host's state first, so a deliberate stop is a silence it expects.

stages.text: Two hooks rather than three: a pre-commit that scans and checks, and a pre-push that refuses main. Commit messages are held to Conventional Commits by a workflow instead of a local hook, since much of what lands here arrives as a dependency bump rather than as somebody typing a message.
stages.title: Before the commit

stages.text: Shared infrastructure is mostly not application code, so the checks are not application checks: formatting, shellcheck, workflow and compose linting, terraform validate against both stacks, the observability kit typechecked and tested, and the deploy script's env-file helpers under bats. A secret scan and Semgrep alongside them.
stages.title: The pull request

stages.text: release-please in simple mode. There is no package to version here — only a tag and a changelog that record what the shared platform now is, which is what the products pin themselves against.
stages.title: The release

stages.text: A published release, or a manual dispatch, packages the tracked files into a bundle, uploads it to S3 and has SSM apply it on the host. The shared stack deploys down exactly the same path as the products sitting on it, which is how that path stays trustworthy: everything exercises it. It restarts the secret store only when that store's own config changed — a mount path carrying the release name used to recreate it on every release.
stages.title: The deploy

platform-ops.problem: Five applications each needed secret storage, translations, an event broker and observability. Duplicating that per repository means five OpenBao instances to unseal and five ways to be inconsistent.
platform-ops.tagline: The shared operations stack every other project attaches to instead of rebuilding.

sity.approach: One plan describes every road as nodes and typed segments. From it the scene builds the geometry it renders and the directed lane graph that vehicles will follow, so the drawing and the data cannot disagree. The terrain follows the roads and the streams (cuttings, embankments, tunnel portals and culverts come from the same centrelines), every dead end finishes at a destination whose parking bays are exported for the simulation, and the city grows from the streets: lots are cut along each frontage and filled with instanced buildings whose facades come from a shader.
decisions: Roads are drawn from the graph rather than the graph fitted to the drawing. A road rendered from the same sampled centreline as its lanes means a vehicle on lane data is on the asphalt, with no second source of truth to reconcile.

Everything repeated is instanced and everything else is merged per material, which keeps the whole 13 km² site under 600 draw calls and 4.6 million triangles with post-processing on. The facade grid is computed in the shader from the instance box, so building variety costs attributes, not geometry.

pieces.text: A ring highway with a tunnel, a cable-stayed bridge and viaducts; a diamond, a dumbbell, a half-diamond, a trumpet and a cloverleaf, plus a road under the viaduct; two motorways that leave the map at its edges: one south with a lane drop, a rest area on its own ramps and a rural overpass, one west through a mountain tunnel with a diamond, a services area and free-flow toll gantries; a downtown grid with bus lanes, left-turn pockets and cycle tracks on the arterials, collectors, a one-way pair, a school zone, roundabouts, a curved riverside collector and two river bridges; a railway with a gated level crossing and a station forecourt, a village loop, a hospital drive and farm lanes; in the mountains a forest road, a valley road to a pass and a switchback col road to an alpine village; and beyond the pass, rural roads through a dense pine forest with a hamlet and a lake and across farmland with a farm village, where brooks are crossed by culverts and small bridges. Each road carries its class rules for lanes, medians, sidewalks and speed, and every dead end is a car park, forecourt, yard or viewpoint.
pieces.title: Road plan

pieces.text: Every lane is a directed polyline with successors, predecessors and neighbours. Junction connectors are generated per allowed turn, roundabouts as circulating arcs, ramps as diverges and merges. Dijkstra routing, path enumeration and invariant checks live on the same graph.
pieces.title: Lane graph

pieces.text: Districts decide what a lot becomes: towers on podiums downtown, brick and plaster blocks, houses with gardens, chalets on the mountain, sheds by the port, hotels on the coast. Facades are a shader over per-instance attributes, so a few thousand buildings cost a handful of draw calls. Forests, street trees, parks, a plaza, an arena, a multi-storey car park, a school, churches, a station, a hospital, hedged fields and a generated farmland grid with farmyards, a manor, a sawmill, a farmers' co-op, a wind farm, a golf course, a campsite, two motorway services, a chairlift, a container terminal, an amusement pier and a beach with its promenade fill the rest, with parked cars in every bay and bus stops on the main streets. A footprint audit keeps buildings off pavements and off each other.
pieces.title: City

pieces.text: Vitest covers the network builder, the lane graph and the city plan without a browser: turn connectors at a crossroads, lane assignment and adjacency, roundabout rings, ramp diverges and merges, invariants and routing. Playwright drives the built site through a debug API: graph invariants, routing between the highway and Main Street, the building-footprint audit, a check that no dead end is left without a destination, city counts, draw-call and triangle budgets, rendered views checked pixel by pixel and kept as screenshots, and the panel against WCAG A and AA.
pieces.title: Verification

automation: Dependabot over npm, the Docker base images and the Actions, grouped weekly with a seven-day cooldown; auto-merge on green for patch and minor, the same policy as the rest of the estate.
CodeQL on every pull request and weekly on main, dependency review, commitlint on the commits and the pull request title, and gitleaks over the full history.

The Playwright suite runs against the production build served by Vite preview, on headless Chromium with software WebGL, on a desktop and a mobile viewport, and keeps a screenshot of every camera view as test output so a change to the city can be reviewed by eye as well as by assertion.

stages.text: gitleaks over the staged diff, then format check, lint, typecheck, unit tests with coverage and the build; commitlint on the message; and a pre-push hook that refuses main. The same hooks as the other repositories.
stages.title: Before the commit

stages.text: Quality, then a Docker smoke test of the nginx image, the Playwright suite — asset pack, lane-graph invariants, routing between the ring highway and Main Street, city counts, performance budgets, pixel samples of every camera view and axe against WCAG A and AA — a licence gate and npm audit on production dependencies, an SBOM and a Trivy scan of the image, and Semgrep.
stages.title: The pull request

stages.text: release-please derives the version and changelog from the conventional commits on main, and publishes the tag when its pull request is merged.
stages.title: The release

stages.text: The image is built and smoke-tested but not shipped: the scene has no users beyond its author until vehicles and traffic devices exist, so there is no host and no deploy workflow yet.
stages.title: No deploy, yet

sity.problem: Simulating smart traffic — adaptive signals, rerouting when a road clogs — needs a city that is credible to look at and a road network a program can drive: lanes with direction, turns, ramps and roundabouts, not a picture of asphalt.
sity.tagline: A coastal city built in Three.js as the ground for smart-traffic simulations, with every road already a lane graph.

trading-bot.approach: Latency-sensitive work lives in Rust crates; orchestration and supervision live in TypeScript. The two halves meet at a control plane, with a Next.js operator console on top.
decisions: Backtesting and live execution consume the same strategy crate, so a result that cannot be reproduced offline is a bug rather than a mystery.
The control-plane keeps a URL version because three Rust services call it across a network and deploy separately; the products that ship their client from the same repository do not.

pieces.text: Separate crates for market data, the strategy engine, execution, and research backtesting, so the backtest and the live path can share the same strategy code.
pieces.title: Rust crates

pieces.text: A TypeScript service coordinating the crates and owning the operational API.
pieces.title: Control plane

pieces.text: A Next.js supervision UI built on Tailwind and Radix, sharing the design system with the other products.
pieces.title: Operator console

automation: Dependabot covers npm, Cargo and both Dockerfiles, so the Rust dependencies get the same weekly attention as the TypeScript ones rather than ageing quietly.
Auto-merge on green for patch and minor; majors wait for a person, in both ecosystems.
CodeQL, dependency review and Semgrep on every pull request — the same gate the production repositories use, because the code will need it before it deploys, not after.

Local development has two modes over one set of containers, across both languages. `local:dev` runs the control plane under `tsx watch`, the console under `next dev` and the three Rust services under `cargo watch`, all fed by `docker compose watch`. The Rust services share one named volume for the cargo target directory, so the dependency artefacts they have in common are compiled once rather than three times: the first build is long, an incremental one is a few seconds.

stages.text: gitleaks over the staged diff and then the workspace checks, commitlint on the message, and a pre-push hook that refuses main. The same three hooks as the rest of the estate, so moving between repositories does not mean learning a different set of local rules.
stages.title: Before the commit

stages.text: Two language lanes running side by side. Rust: cargo fmt --check, a lock check that refuses a Cargo.lock disagreeing with the manifests, clippy with warnings denied, and the workspace test suite. TypeScript: format, typecheck, build and tests for the control plane and the operator console. A third lane stands a real PostgreSQL up under Compose and runs the control plane's trade projection against it. Around them, a secret scan, compose manifests rendered against a placeholder env, supply chain and Semgrep.
stages.title: The pull request

stages.text: One version across two languages. release-please bumps both package.json files, the Cargo workspace and both lockfiles from the same conventional commits, so a crate and the console that drives it can never claim different versions of the same release, and no build after a release rewrites a lock.
stages.title: The release

stages.text: There is no deploy workflow. The bot runs from Compose on a machine somebody is watching, and automating the path to production before a strategy has earned trust would only make it faster to ship something that should not be running.
stages.title: No deploy, deliberately

trading-bot.problem: A strategy that runs unattended needs two very different things: a fast, predictable execution path, and a supervision surface a human can read at a glance. Building both in one language means compromising one of them.
trading-bot.tagline: A trading platform split between a Rust hot path and a TypeScript control plane with an operator console.

0.note: Daily first, then fluent enough to be useful.
